topicTitle: NEB Class 11 Chemistry — Classification Of Elements And Periodic Table — 2021
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: How does the Modern Periodic Law differ from Mendeleev's Periodic Law? State any three points of difference.
questions.solution:
| Mendeleev's Periodic Law | Modern Periodic Law |
| --- | --- |
| Properties are a periodic function of **atomic mass**. | Properties are a periodic function of **atomic number** ($Z$). |
| Periodic table had **8 groups** (or 8 + 8 + ... columns) and periods of **irregular** length, ranging from 2 to 8 elements. | Table has **18 groups** and periods of regular length, the number of elements increasing from 2 to 32 as $Z$ increases. |
| Positions of several elements could not be correctly predicted, and there were no **isotopes** concept. | Correctly accommodates **isotopes** (they have the same $Z$) and correctly predicts the positions of elements **discovered after Mendeleev**. |

Mendeleev successfully predicted the existence of eka-aluminium (gallium) and eka-silicon (germanium), but he could not explain the positions of the noble gases or the lanthanides.

Thus the modern law corrected the mass basis, gave the group/period structure, and removed all the anomalies left in the periodic table.
questions.knowledgeNote: The Modern Periodic Law makes atomic number, not atomic mass, the basis of periodicity, giving 18 groups and regular periods.
questions.answer: **Mendeleev's law:** the properties of elements are a periodic function of their **atomic masses**. **Modern periodic law:** the properties of elements are a periodic function of their **atomic numbers**. **Three differences:** (1) **basis** — atomic mass (Mendeleev) vs atomic number (modern); the modern law is grounded in nuclear charge, the quantity that actually determines electronic configuration; (2) **anomalies removed** — Mendeleev had to place pairs out of mass order (Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I); by atomic number they fall into their correct groups naturally, with no inversions; (3) **isotopes explained** — isotopes of an element have different masses but the same atomic number, so they occupy one position in the modern table (Mendeleev's mass-based table could not accommodate them); additionally, the modern table's blocks (s/p/d/f) follow directly from electron configuration, giving the long form its structure. **Deep point:** the change from mass to number is the change from a property that misorders (mass) to the property that causes periodicity (Z ⟹ configuration ⟹ properties) — every improvement in the table flows from that single correction.
